statement: Some bread poses a higher choking risk to babies than other types of bread.
transcript: Did you know that some bread is actually a higher choking risk than others for babies? Avoid soft breads as they can form a gummy mass that actually increases the risk of choking. Instead, opt for well-toasted bread or the large heel of a thick, crusty loaf. Bread that has some resistance stands up to the powerful suck and grip of young babies, and it also offers valuable opportunities for lots of biting and tearing practice. When it comes to sliced bread, serve it toasted and cut into wide strips. And if you want to top it with something, aim for very thin spreads, especially when it comes to nut butters, as these can get extra sticky in baby's mouth. Try to avoid breads that include additional choking hazards like large nuts or seeds, and avoid honey as an ingredient before 12 months.

statement: Early introduction of peanut between four to six months of age can reduce the risk of peanut allergy in children.
transcript: you're a parent and you've seen these headlines about peanut allergy and want to understand a little bit more about the science and the research behind it, listen on, especially if you're feeling confused or conflicted about what to do around weaning. Loads of you have asked me to comment on this news article and so what I want to point out that the news article is based on this paper here. Now this paper that has just come out in March of this year has basically pulled together data from really good quality scientific studies that look at early introduction to peanut in infants and the reduction of peanut allergy risk. Now just to say these studies we knew about already they include the LEAP study and the EAT study but what this study does is pull all of that information together and models the impact of early introduction of peanut into children's diets between four to six months of age and the potential impact this will have on peanut allergy prevalence overall. What the model very clearly shows is that the preventative benefit of early introduction of peanut allergy is that it can reduce the risk of peanut allergy to children. So early introduction of peanuts decreases as the age of introduction increases so that goes with a message that we've been giving for a long time which is do not delay introduction of these foods including peanut as an allergenic food during weaning. The key thing that people are finding conflicting particularly when you're looking at introduction of solids is that in the UK the recommended guidance is that we commence solids with children at around six months of age. However the researchers here are looking for consideration of introduction of foods like peanut in this case earlier between four to six months of age. So we are yet to know whether weeding guidance will change based on this data that's certainly what they're calling for in terms of an important public health message. It may well be that there are specific recommendations made for children considered at higher risk of peanut allergy and then population level recommendations. It's likely that there will have to be a balance between considering a child's readiness for weaning, risk of peanut allergy and other food allergies and essentially all of the other information that we have about introduction of solid foods already. I'd love to know at what age did you introduce peanuts or have you not introduced peanuts yet and if so what's holding you back from doing it? okay
